images.title: The only way is up
images.caption: Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong, China
images.desc: Welcome to Hong Kong, home to the world's largest collection of skyscrapers. Those pictured here tower above Victoria Harbour, whose deep waters allowed the island to develop as a busy trading port. Ships carrying tea, silk and other goods have passed through since the 1840s, but growth rocketed in the decades after World War II, fuelling a construction boom. With little flat land available between the harbour and the hills, developers had to build upward, creating this distinctive skyline. In 2026, Hong Kong has 569 completed buildings at least 150 metres tall — more than any other city.

images.title: Hidden depths
images.caption: Ice on Abraham Lake in Alberta
images.desc: Dawn's first light is reflected on the frozen surface of Abraham Lake, framed by Rocky Mountains peaks. In winter, this picturesque lake in Alberta is famous for its frozen bubbles of methane gas, trapped beneath the ice. Strong winds keep the surface clear of snow, offering winter-long views. Come spring, when the ice thaws, the gas escapes into the atmosphere.

images.title: Architecture without an architect
images.caption: North Window, Arches National Park, Moab, Utah
images.desc: Just north of Moab, Utah, Arches National Park is home to more than 2,000 natural sandstone arches – the densest concentration of arches in the world. Today's image, North Window, is one of the best-known formations in the park's Windows Section, where towering fins, openings and sculpted sandstone create a landscape that looks almost architectural.

images.title: A forest full of wonder
images.caption: The Atlantic Forest, Brazil
images.desc: The Atlantic Forest is one of the world's great biodiversity hotspots, stretching along much of Brazil's Atlantic coast and into Argentina and Paraguay. Its landscape includes tropical and subtropical forests, mangroves and coastal habitats, providing a home for around 20,000 plant species and an extraordinary variety of wildlife, including jaguars and golden lion tamarins. Much of the forest has disappeared over the centuries, but it continues to play an important role in storing carbon and providing fresh water for millions of people across the region.

images.title: Licensed to chill
images.caption: Aerial view of Rose Island, The Bahamas
images.desc: Rose Island is a picture-perfect escape in The Bahamas, where lush greenery meets some of the most vibrant blue waters in the Caribbean. Located just a short boat ride from Nassau, this peaceful cay is known for its pristine beaches, crystal-clear shallows and relaxed island atmosphere. Movie fans may recognize it as a filming location from the 1965 James Bond adventure Thunderball, but today Rose Island's biggest attractions are its natural beauty and unique wildlife, including its famous swimming pigs. Viewed from above, the island showcases the dazzling colours that make The Bahamas world-renowned, with turquoise lagoons, sandy shoals and clear waters creating a breathtaking tropical landscape.

images.title: Where art finds its rhythm
images.caption: Historic district of Triana, Seville, Spain
images.desc: Cross the Guadalquivir River and discover Triana, one of Seville’s most vibrant neighbourhoods. Connected to the city’s historic centre by the iconic Triana Bridge since the 19th century, this riverside district is known for its colourful ceramics, flamenco heritage and lively local culture. Brightly decorated buildings, traditional tile workshops and bustling markets give Triana a character all its own. Stroll along Calle Betis for scenic river views, explore streets lined with artisan studios, or simply soak up the neighbourhood’s welcoming atmosphere. While Seville’s famous landmarks are just steps away, Triana offers a unique glimpse into the traditions, creativity and everyday life that help define Andalusia.

images.title: A celebration that shines
images.caption: Diwali (Festival of Lights)
images.desc: Diwali, the Festival of Lights, is celebrated by millions of people around the world, including vibrant communities across Canada. Rooted in the Sanskrit word dipavali, meaning “row of lights,” the festival symbolizes the triumph of light over darkness and hope over adversity. Families and friends gather to light diyas and lanterns, create colourful rangoli, share sweets and take part in prayers and celebrations. While traditions vary across regions and faiths, Diwali is widely recognized as a time of reflection, gratitude and togetherness. As communities across Canada come together to celebrate, the festival continues to brighten neighbourhoods, workplaces and schools with its message of unity, joy and renewal.

images.title: The giant that came back
images.caption: Bison
images.desc: One of North America's most remarkable animals, the bison is a powerful symbol of strength, resilience and conservation. Weighing as much as 900 kilograms (2,000 pounds) and capable of running up to 55 km/h (35 mph), bison are surprisingly agile. Despite being commonly called buffalo, American bison are a distinct species known for their massive shoulder hump, curved horns and shaggy coats that help them thrive through harsh winters. Once pushed to the brink of extinction, bison have made an inspiring comeback thanks to conservation efforts across Canada and the United States, making them a powerful example of successful wildlife recovery.
